news.title: Nashville Airport Could Soon Carry Dolly Parton's Name, Tennessee Governor Announces
news.text: Los Angeles: Nashville could soon have an airport named after one of Tennessee's most beloved stars. Three days after the death of the 80-year-old country music icon Dolly Parton, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has announced plans to rename Nashville International Airport in her honour, Variety reported.Governor Lee and the Nashville International Airport officials announced the proposal in a joint statement on Friday, saying they intend to begin the process of changing the airport's name.Dolly Parton, who was born in rural Tennessee and later moved to Nashville, had won 10 Grammy awards and sold 100 million records worldwide, including hits like Coat of Many Colors, 9 to 5, Jolene, and I Will Always Love You.Calling Parton "Tennessee's favourite daughter," Lee said the airport would be a fitting place to honour her life and work."Dolly Parton's extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state. At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state's favourite daughter and greet travellers with the enduring legacy of Dolly's music, generosity, faith and kindness," he said.According to the statement, Parton's team is aware of the proposal and supports continuing talks about the possible name change. The singer had a long connection with Tennessee through her music and charitable work, including the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library.According to Variety, the proposal to rename the airport was first made last year after a petition was started following a separate proposal to rename the airport after US President Donald Trump. The petition gained a large number of new signatures following Parton's death.Doug Kreulen, president and CEO of the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority, said Parton's legacy was closely linked to the welcoming spirit of Nashville. He said, "Dolly's remarkable legacy reminds us that what makes Nashville special is our ability to welcome people from every walk of life. Sheunderstood that dignity, kindness and opportunity should never be defined by where you come from or your socioeconomic status."Nashville Mayor Freddie O'Connell also backed the proposal. He recalled Parton's plans for a hotel and museum in the city and said the airport could now become another way for the city to honour her."Dolly was in the process of working with us on a remarkable hotel and museum SongTeller, that she called her love letter to Nashville. Now it's our turn to share a love letter to Dolly, by renaming Nashville International Airport to Dolly Parton International Airport in Nashville," O'Connell wrote o social media.The proposed name change will be discussed at the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority's meeting on September 17.

news.title: Interest rates, fish and Donald Trump on Icelanders' minds as nation goes to referendum on EU
news.text:
High interest rates and inflation, a fishing industry under threat and the shadow of Donald Trump are on the minds of Icelanders as the country goes to a referendum this weekend to decide whether it should restart negotiations on joining the European Union.

If this tiny island nation of almost 400,000 people chooses 'yes', they would have a second vote later to seal the deal reached between Reykjavik and Brussels.

Or the people could reject it and keep the status quo.

A Gallup poll this month found voters split on restarting talks with the EU: 46 per cent said they would vote yes and 46 per cent no, with 8 per cent undecided.

Other polls show a majority against actually joining the bloc.

For Icelanders who support the 'yes' side the most compelling argument is around creating economic opportunities and improving cost of living.

Living standards and wages are high, but so are inflation and interest rates.

Economics student Óðinn Freyr Baldursson, 21, is saving up to buy his first home.

"The interest rates for mortgages, regular mortgages for homes, are around 9 per cent here in Iceland," Mr Baldursson said.

"Which is more than two times higher than most other places in Europe, and that's the main reason why owning a house here in Iceland is so, so tough."

He said he believed that if Iceland joined the EU and replaced the volatile krona with the euro, interest rates and inflation would come down.

"Just based off of the experience of other countries joining the EU, we can expect that interest rates will decrease by 3 to 4, maybe 5 per cent," he said.

The 'no' side fervently disagrees that joining the EU would solve this.

"Telling people 'we just need to go into the EU because we have so high interest rates, because we have so high inflation' [is wrong], because we have to deal with inflation and the interest rates either way," 'no' campaigner Steinar Ingi Kolbeins, 29, told 7.30.

"For me, that's just that the government is not doing their job."

He said even if Iceland was to have a seat at the table in Brussels, he doubted his country's officials would have much of an impact because it would have fewer seats than the larger nations.

"We have to think about what does the seat at the table look like? What's the size of the chair? And what's the trade-off? What are we letting go of for that seat at the table?" Mr Kolbeins said.

His colleague Magnea Gná Jóhannsdóttir, also 29, said she was motivated to vote 'no' because she wanted "decisions to be made in Iceland by Icelanders".

"I don't want to sell the EU the right of our natural resources or fisheries or farming and all the other things that are part of the European Union," she said.

"And [having negotiations] is a not a journey that's free. It costs money. It costs the time of the government."

The government though, argues the time and investment would be worth it and provide more opportunities for the people.

Fears for fishing industry

On the west coast of Iceland, the Snaefellsnes Peninsula is famous for its appearance in the hit TV show Game of Thrones but it is also home to a thriving fishing industry.

Sustainable fishing is central to Iceland's identity and economy — only Icelandic ships can fish within the 200 nautical miles (321 kilometres) of the island and foreign companies can't own fish processing facilities.

If Iceland joins the EU, those in the fishing industry fear the bloc's Common Fisheries Policy will mean these exclusive waters will become a free-for-all.

Arnar Kristjánsson's family business, G.RUN, has been fishing in them for more than 70 years.

G.RUN is the biggest employer in the small town of Grundarfjörður — 80 of the roughly 800 residents work for the company.

Mr Kristjánsson is firmly against joining the EU.

"The big companies in Europe will swallow up all these small companies and for small towns like this, there will be no more fish production," the third-generation owner said.

"Iceland tries to use our fish stocks in a way that they can keep producing, [but] Europe has not done that. Many of their fish stocks are in a very bad shape and we don't like to have that here."

Prominent 'yes' supporter and Reykjavik MP Dagur B Eggertsson said fishing history "matters very much" and Icelandic officials would fight for exemptions so the industry could be protected.

"The kind of detailed plans of how to handle this have been met with the kind of words of flexibility and openness on the EU's behalf," Mr Eggertsson told 7.30.

"Some people say [exemptions] are out of the question but one of the arguments for a 'yes' in this referendum is exactly to go into negotiations."

Former president of Iceland from 1996 to 2016, Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, said he believed exemptions would not happen.

"The core element in the whole EU existence is the commonality of the rules applying to everyone, every country, every economy, so you can't perhaps say, 'Let's try to see what we can get,' no," Mr Grímsson told 7.30.

He said he feared Iceland would be taking a huge step backwards if it was to eventually join the EU.

"It took the generation of my parents and grandparents 100 years to gain independence [from Denmark], full control over our powers, the right to negotiate with other countries, to be a sovereign state," the former president said.

'No' campaigners see multiple threats

Iceland has been proudly independent since it broke away from Denmark in 1944.

It first looked at EU entry 17 years ago after the global financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking sector, but walked away after disagreements on several policies, including fishing.

But the world has changed a lot since then.

Iceland sits opposite Greenland, just beside the Arctic Circle, a region the US, Russia and China all want to exploit for resources and new shipping channels as the polar ice melts due to climate change.

US President Donald Trump's ongoing campaign to slap tariffs on allies, and his threats to annex Greenland, before confusing it with Iceland multiple times in a speech at January's Davos Economic Forum, have startled people here.

These developments have prompted some Icelandic policymakers to seek deeper security and economic cooperation with European partners.

Iceland's already a member of the defence alliance NATO and some European trade agreements, but now the coalition government wants extra reinforcement with EU membership as well.

"Wars are not just wars fought with weapons. We also see trade wars going on and threats of tariffs being used. Tariffs are being weaponised.

"So where should we, as Icelanders, seek tighter bonds? I see that within the EU."

The EU will be watching Saturday's referendum closely.

Given how peaceful, prosperous and well-positioned Iceland is, this Nordic nation would be seen by many in Brussels as a very good get.

But if the 'yes' vote gets up, the path forward will be tricky — negotiations will require delicate diplomacy and calculated compromise.

For the Icelandic people though, the vote is not about what is in it for the EU, but all about what is in it for them.

news.summary: Iceland is a nation divided as its people go to a referendum this weekend to decide whether it should restart negotiations on joining the European Union.

news.title: Iranian leaders admit economic toll of war with US as trade drops 35%
news.text:
Iranian leaders are acknowledging the economic toll of war with the United States, with the supreme leader calling on the government to address the hardship while the president reported foreign trade has shrunk 35 per cent due to the American sanctions and blockade.
The warnings came even as other leaders threaten the US with military retaliation and declarations that the Iranian navy maintains control of the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway giving Iran ‌leverage through its ability to disrupt global energy markets.
With the war now at the six-month mark, and negotiations at an impasse, President Donald Trump’s administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an “economic D-Day”.
Washington has warned countries to cut their business ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions – though the Treasury Department stopped short of imposing penalties against major Iranian trade partners such as China and India, which could have repercussions for the US and global economies.

The US Treasury Department did impose sanctions on Egypt’s Banque Misr for doing business with Tehran, proposing a rule that would cut off ⁠the bank’s branches in the United Arab Emirates from dollar transactions.
Egypt’s central bank said it and the foreign ministry were in contact with US officials concerning the matter, adding ‌the measure was limited to Banque Misr UAE’s US dollar transactions with correspondent banks only.
US Treasury officials separately issued sanctions targeting one entity based in Hong Kong and one person linked to Iran’s Bank Melli, according to a notice posted on the department’s website.
The sanctions drive ‌compounds the toll of the war on Iran’s economy, where annual inflation hit 66 per cent last month.
Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured ⁠and has not been seen publicly since ⁠the February 28 attack that killed his father, former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, called on the government to tackle the economic hardship.
“There is the need to seriously address the chain of economic and livelihood challenges, ‌such as inflation, unemployment, management of prices and the market for goods and services,” a written statement attributed to Khamenei said.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that Iranian exports and imports slumped nearly 35 per cent because of US sanctions ‌and a ‌naval blockade of Iranian ports.
But he said Iran was able to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the short-lived memorandum of understanding that the US ‌and Iran signed in June, when Washington permitted Iranian oil sales.
With the US focused on its economic pressure campaign, others have sought to revive diplomatic efforts to end the ⁠war.
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani met Iranian leaders in Tehran on Thursday. He said he had stressed during the meeting the importance of ⁠returning to the pre-war status of open shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi on Friday described the talks with Al Thani as “creative”.
Qatar, a US ally and Gulf neighbour of Iran, and Pakistan helped broker the June memorandum of understanding that led to a brief ceasefire before disagreements over the strait caused it to unravel.
US ‌military commanders say American forces have cleared sea mines from the strait that had been laid months ago by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Trump has repeatedly said the strait is open, but the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ navy said in a statement that such claims “are an obvious lie”, reiterating that the waterway remained closed to ships without Iranian permission.
Preliminary shipping data released on Friday showed that only seven commodity vessels had transited the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, down from 17 a day earlier and below the 10-day average of 15.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi on Friday described the talks with Al Thani as “creative”.
Qatar, a US ally and Gulf neighbour of Iran, and Pakistan helped broker the June memorandum of understanding that led to a brief ceasefire before disagreements over the strait caused it to unravel.
US ‌military commanders say American forces have cleared sea mines from the strait that had been laid months ago by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Trump has repeatedly said the strait is open, but the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ navy said in a statement that such claims “are an obvious lie”, reiterating that the waterway remained closed to ships without Iranian permission.
Preliminary shipping data released on Friday showed that only seven commodity vessels had transited the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, down from 17 a day earlier and below the 10-day average of 15.

news.title: Trump says US is taking partial control of Venezuela's vast oil reserves
news.text:
Donald Trump has said the US has entered into an agreement with Venezuela to take control of a fifth of the country's oil reserves.

The US president provided few details about the agreement, ​saying only that the US had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's proven oil reserves through a partnership with private business.

The new deal represents a dramatic expansion of the US role ⁠in Venezuela's oil industry.

In a post on his Truth Social platform, Mr Trump said the deal had been negotiated by secretary of state Marco Rubio, defence secretary Pete Hegseth and Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodriguez.

"At my direction, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, working closely with Highly Respected Interim ​President of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, and, through a partnership with private business, have secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 ‌BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer," Mr Trump said.

Mr Trump added that the transaction "MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves".

Mr Rubio said the agreement would usher in billions in private investment into Venezuela and lead to lower gas prices in the US.

"This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people," he wrote on X.

Ms Rodriguez also welcomed the agreement, saying it would boost the Venezuelan economy and "have a significant impact on our nation's revival".

Her government said in a statement that the deal involves the development of 17 fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels.

It said the agreement could draw $100bn in investment into Venezuela's oil industry and yield over $209bn in taxes for Caracas.

The announcement comes almost nine months after the US military carried out an operation to capture Venezuela's then president Nicolas Maduro to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges in the US.

Mr Trump is facing increasing pressure as the US midterm elections loom, and gas prices have spiked because of the war with Iran, which the US and Israel started six months ago.

Venezuela has one of the largest oil reserves in the world, amounting to about 17% of the world's supply, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Unlike other parts of the world, where geologists have to search for untapped oil, the reserves under Venezuela's soil are largely mapped and known - but because of dilapidated infrastructure, the country only produces about 1% of the world's oil.
